title: Newcastle increase season ticket prices for fourth successive season
content:
Newcastle United have announced a five per cent increase in general-admission season ticket prices for the fourth season in succession.

For the 2026-27 campaign, that represents an above-inflation rise year on year, while there is an increase of 15 per cent for seats in premium bar sections. The disability ticket discount has reduced from 50 per cent to 25 per cent, though accessibility holders are still eligible to get a free ticket for a personal assistant.

According to the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), which is the measure by which the UK government sets the Bank of England’s target for inflation, prices in Britain rose by an average of three per cent in the 12 months to January 2026. Most season ticket holders will face a price hike above inflation, many significantly above that level.

In January, having been asked by the official Fan Advisory Board (FAB) and Newcastle United Supporters Trust (NUST) for greater transparency, CEO David Hopkinson confirmed via the club’s website that the club have “over 35,000 season ticket holders” which “equates to approximately 70 per cent of home fans” at a typical Premier League match at St James’ Park. Work is being undertaken to create a season ticket waiting list, too.

Hopkinson told the club’s website on the increases: “We fully understand this will not be popular news, and it is not a decision we take lightly. But the reality is that without making responsible increases, we cannot continue progressing or competing at the level we all expect and aspire to.

“In the current financial landscape, we must balance affordability for our fans with the need to generate the revenue required to remain competitive. After this adjustment, our general admission ticket prices will remain competitive in terms of value against other Premier League clubs.

“I also want to be clear about how we spend our revenue. The ultimate aim is to reinvest it directly into the areas that matter most: building a successful team, enhancing your matchday experience, and strengthening the infrastructure that supports long‑term success.”

A statement from the FAB read: “The FAB unanimously advised the club that there should be no increase to season ticket pricing and are disappointed the club has decided to go ahead with an increase.”

Ticket prices are one source used to maximise revenue streams, which Newcastle believe they must do to realise their ambitions in a footballing landscape governed by financial rules. The higher Newcastle’s income from football activities, the more they can spend.

The Premier League’s profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) are being replaced by squad cost ratio (SCR) from next season, with expenditure directly linked to revenue. Clubs can spend up to 85 per cent of their football-related revenue in the Premier League on player wages, transfers and agents fees, while in UEFA competitions that figure is restricted to 70 per cent.

Before the 2025-26 season, thousands of Newcastle supporters had to stomach five per cent rises on top of the ending of a long-term season ticket price freeze. Mike Ashley, the previous owner, had introduced fixed-term price freezes ahead of the 2010-11 campaign, initially for a 10-year period, but that was extended.

All general season ticket holders will face a five per cent rise, with those who were not previously on the long-term freeze having already absorbed annual hikes at the same rate for the previous three seasons.

Newcastle insist they will reinvest some of the money in higher-visibility screens inside the St James’  bowl “to improve score/time and VAR communication”, while upgrades are also being made to audio systems, kiosks and seating.

The FAB statement continued: “We are pleased that our engagement with the club resulted in some positive outcomes. The club has agreed to reconsider plans to introduce an additional range of booking fees and has also decided not to proceed with proposals to remove certain student discounts.

“The FAB also advised against changing the disability discounts but suggested working with NUDSA (Newcastle United Disabled Supporters Association) on this sensitive change.”

Financial regulations have restricted Newcastle’s post-takeover rise and the club have long been adamant that every revenue stream must be maximised to try and bridge the gap to those above, something which Hopkinson has reiterated repeatedly since his appointment in September.

However, for supporters who have already seen three annual price hikes of five per cent, an above-inflation rise will hit many hard during a cost-of-living crisis in one of the poorest areas of the country.

With matchday revenue (£50.1million, $66.9m) also now the lowest of the club’s three main income streams, according to the club’s accounts for 2023-24 — still their most recent financial results, with those for 2024-25 expected to be released within the next month — and only producing 15.6 per cent of their entire £320.3m ($427.36m) annual revenue, it is questionable how much of a difference this five per cent rise will actually make.

A very rough estimate would be that this generates somewhere between £1.5m ($2m) and £2.5m ($3.34m).

Newcastle insist every penny counts in a PSR/soon-to-be-SCR world and will allow the club to bolster Eddie Howe’s squad, but this decision will prompt anger and resentment among their fanbase.

While the club’s desire to be transparent should be welcomed and applauded, worryingly, financial rules and the need to be competitive by maximising revenues is once again being used as a justification for increasing ticket prices. Newcastle are far from the only club to do this, however, and it brings the present and future regulations under even closer scrutiny.

If a byproduct of the Premier League and UEFA rules is that clubs can use the excuse of PSR/SCR to raise ticket prices for their fans, does that not suggest that fundamentally there is something morally questionable about the entire system?
